read: partial: main text (pages 1-10) and appendices B and D.2 in full; appendices C, D.1, D.3 and the result tables and figures skimmed for their EngTrace coverage
venue_now: arXiv 2605.15393v1, 14 May 2026, cs.LG; FAIR at Meta preprint dated 18 May 2026 (p.1); no venue
what_it_is: LPDS is a method, not a new benchmark. It scores how hard a logic-preserving variation of a symbolic-template problem is for a given model, by the distance of the model's response from its own correctly answered responses (minimum normalised Levenshtein distance, or Mahalanobis distance of mean hidden states), and uses beam search over the template's slots to find the variations that maximise that difficulty (p.1, p.4, p.6). It applies this to 100 templates each from GSM-Symbolic, FinChain and EngTrace's first release (taken from EngTrace's GitHub, with templates split where a binary variable changed the solution structure) with seven open models, five-shot chain-of-thought and greedy decoding, scoring final answers only (p.3-4, p.16). Beam-searched variations give accuracy drops up to five times larger than random sampling, so random sampling overstates robustness; fine-tuning on harder variations gives more consistent gains (p.1, p.7-9).
domain: grade-school math (GSM-Symbolic), finance (FinChain), and engineering (EngTrace's chemical, electrical and mechanical templates) (p.3, p.16)
size: 100 templates per dataset; 1,000 variations per template in the metric study, 100,000 per dataset (p.5); up to T x w x b explored variations per template in the search (p.7); 7 models: Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3.1-8B and 70B, Qwen-2.5-7B, 32B and 72B, Phi-4 (p.3). On EngTrace: five models in the metric study (p.27-28) and three in the search and robustness results (p.24, p.34)
source_of_items: generated from existing symbolic templates (GSM-Symbolic, FinChain, EngTrace); the EngTrace templates were split and their numeric ranges narrowed by the LPDS authors (p.15-16)
instances: generated: variations sampled and searched from the templates (p.5-7)
has_gold_traces: partial: the templates' ground-truth reasoning is used only as fine-tuning targets (p.9); evaluation is final-answer only, and the difficulty metrics compare a response with the model's own correct responses, not with gold traces (p.4)
evaluation: final answer: the last number in the response (models are told to give it after '####'), exact match for GSM-Symbolic, |y_hat - y| <= 1e-6 + 0.01|y| for FinChain and EngTrace (p.4); AUC and odds ratios for the difficulty metrics (p.5); error rates under beam search against random sampling (p.7-8, p.24); a difficulty-robustness score, the normalised area under the accuracy-quantile curve (p.25, p.34)
contamination_measures: generated variations; the authors read the drops as partly reflecting superficial cues and possible contamination (p.2, p.8)

engtrace_use.explanation: Belongs in: the introduction, where symbolic templates and contamination resistance are argued (beside GSM-Symbolic), with a pointer in Limitations. Candidate, not cited in the May paper. It uses EngTrace's first-release templates as one of its three datasets and names EngTrace (Gull et al., 2025) among studies that evaluate a randomly sampled subset of template instances, a practice it argues can overestimate robustness (p.2). It finds EngTrace variations the hardest of its three template sets for the three small models it searches on them (p.24-25, p.34). This bears directly on how the revision describes instance sampling and robustness.

suggested_wording: LPDS (Mondorf et al., 2026) searches the variation space of symbolic templates, including 100 adapted from EngTrace's first release, for the variations a model finds hardest, and finds larger accuracy drops than random sampling yields, so randomly drawn instances can overstate robustness.
facts_to_cite: difficulty of a variation is measured by the distance of a response from the model's correct responses (Levenshtein; Mahalanobis on hidden states); for Llama-3.1-8B the Mahalanobis distance predicts errors with AUC 0.74 to 0.80 across the three datasets, 0.78 on EngTrace (p.4-5)
beam search over template slots finds variations with accuracy drops up to five times larger than random sampling (p.1, p.7-8)
uses 100 templates each from GSM-Symbolic, FinChain and EngTrace's first release; EngTrace templates were split where a binary variable changed the solution structure (p.3, p.16)
seven open models from 3B to 72B, five-shot chain-of-thought, greedy decoding, final answers scored with a 1% relative tolerance on EngTrace (p.3-4)
on EngTrace, error rates under beam search exceed those under random sampling: 74.3% vs 69.2% (Llama-3.2-3B), 69.5% vs 63.7% (Llama-3.1-8B), 49.9% vs 42.6% (Qwen-2.5-7B) (p.24)
performance drops fastest on EngTrace variations: difficulty-robustness scores of 0.24, 0.30 and 0.51 on EngTrace against 0.54, 0.71 and 0.82 on GSM-Symbolic for the same three models (p.25, p.34)
names EngTrace among studies that evaluate randomly sampled instances, which can overestimate robustness (p.2)
fine-tuning on harder variations gives more consistent robustness gains (shown on GSM-Symbolic and FinChain) (p.9, p.26)
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: symbolic templates with ground-truth reasoning, EngTrace's own among them (p.3, p.16); generated instances; tolerance-based final-answer checking. Lacks: any step-level evaluation (final answer only, p.4); human validation; new engineering items. EngTrace's position: its 15 instances per template are taken round-robin across reasoning-path and answer-form groups from the template's first 100 draws (state brief), not chosen adversarially, so LPDS's critique of random sampling applies to it. What EngTrace adds: trace-level evaluation, two new branches and certified templates; but the revision should cite LPDS where it discusses robustness, and should not claim robustness to the hardest variations of a template.
notes: (1) LPDS used the first-release EngTrace (Gull et al., 2025, arXiv 2511.01650; 90 templates, three branches), taken from GitHub (p.11, p.16). It split templates whose binary variable changes the asked quantity, giving more than 90, and selected 100 of those (p.16): its '100 EngTrace templates' are its own derived templates, not 100 of EngTrace's. (2) Its Figure 24 is headed 'EngChain Template' while the caption says EngTrace (p.34); EngChain was the title of EngTrace's arXiv v1 (search notes), so this is not a different benchmark. The figure's Step 4 shows sin(sqrt({initial_vel_ms} / {mass} * t)), and the stiffness range ends '19999, 200000' (p.34); the repository template has used omega_n in both terms since its first commit (108b0d6, 2025-09-18), so these are LPDS transcription errors, not EngTrace defects. (3) EngTrace coverage is partial: Qwen-2.5-72B and Phi-4 were not run on EngTrace (Tables 10-11, p.28-29); the beam-versus-random error rates and robustness scores cover Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B only (p.24, p.34); fine-tuning uses GSM-Symbolic and FinChain only (p.9, p.26). (4) The high error rates on EngTrace under random sampling (42.6-69.2%) come from 3B-8B models under five-shot prompting with a 1% tolerance and single-number answers (p.4, p.16, p.24), so they say little about the revised roster. (5) The search note's 'accuracy falls fastest on EngTrace variations' is supported (p.25), for those three models.
